title: House Robber
statement:
You're given a list `nums` where nums[i] is the amount of money inside the i-th house along a street. You may rob any set of houses, but you must not rob two houses that are next to each other. Return the largest total you can rob.

An empty street gives 0.

Constraints: 0 <= len(nums) <= 400; 0 <= nums[i] <= 400.

examples.explanation: Rob the houses holding 9 and 8. Houses 1 and 3 aren't neighbours.
Rob the first, fourth and last houses: 4 + 9 + 4. Taking every other house reaches at most 11.
A single house is simply robbed.

hints: Look at just the last house on the street. What are your two choices for it, and what part of the problem is left in each case?
If you rob house i, which neighbouring houses become off limits? If you skip it, what changes?
Try [2, 1, 1, 2] and [10, 1, 1, 10, 1, 1, 10]. Does robbing every other house always win?
Define best(i) as the most money from the first i houses. How does it relate to best(i-1) and best(i-2)?
That recurrence only looks two steps back, so two running values can replace the whole table.
followUps: What are the time and space complexity of your solution, and where could you save space?
Why doesn't robbing every other house (or greedily taking the biggest house) work?
How would you return which houses you robbed, not just the total?
What if the houses were arranged in a circle so the first and last are neighbours?
What if you must rob at least one house out of every three in a row?
idealAnswerPoints: Frames each house as a choice: rob it and add best(i-2), or skip it and keep best(i-1)
Writes best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + nums[i]) with sensible base cases
Notes only two previous values are needed and reduces space to O(1)
Handles the empty and single-house cases without special clutter
Rejects the alternate-houses and take-the-biggest greedy ideas with a counterexample
weakAnswerSigns: Sums the even-indexed or odd-indexed houses and returns the larger one
Greedily robs the largest house first, which fails on [2, 1, 1, 2]
Plain recursion with no memoisation that times out on 400 houses
Crashes on an empty list or a one-house list

rubric.correctness: Maximum total on every test, including empty input, one or two houses, equal values and cases where skipping two houses in a row is best.
rubric.efficiency: Linear time. Exponential recursion fails the long inputs; O(1) space is the target.
rubric.code_quality: A clear recurrence, meaningful names for the two running values, and no special-casing beyond what the loop needs.
rubric.communication: States the take-or-skip decision before coding and checks it against a counterexample to greedy.
